passage: The corridor outside the viva room was loud with first-years, and Vijay had ten minutes to spare when Sarita caught his sleeve. "Vijay bhaiya, you never fail at anything! How do you do it?" Two other juniors leaned in, waiting. He could feel how nice it would be to just nod. Instead he laughed and said, "I failed two papers in my first year. I nearly quit. I sat in the library for a whole month with a friend who explained things to me." Sarita blinked. "Really?" "Really. Don't put me on a shelf, I fall off it." He glanced at the clock, waved, and went in for his viva, a little nervous, and glad he had said it.

qa.q: What did Sarita ask Vijay in the corridor?
qa.a: Sarita asked how he never failed at anything.

qa.q: What did Vijay feel as the juniors leaned in, and what did he decide?
qa.a: He felt how nice it would be to just nod and be admired, but he chose to be honest about his failures instead.

qa.q: What could Vijay do to keep the juniors' admiration healthy?
qa.a: He can keep sharing honest stories about setbacks and what helped him, and avoid using their admiration to get favours.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Vijay after his answer?
qa.a: Sarita may be surprised but also encouraged, learning that even someone Sarita looks up to failed and recovered. Sarita's "Really?" shows the picture of him shifting.

grounding: Juniors treat the protagonist as perfect; he stays honest about his flaws and does not let it inflate him.

passage: The first-years on Nandini's hostel floor in Bengaluru called her 'akka' and asked her about everything: which elective, which tailor, whether to forgive a roommate. Ganga, the youngest, copied her study timetable down to the tea breaks and once said, 'You never get anything wrong.' Nandini laughed, but the line stayed with her. It would have been easy to let it grow. Ganga already offered to fetch her mess dinner and iron her kurtas. That evening, when Ganga came to show her a failed test and apologised for 'letting you down', Nandini pulled her own first-semester marksheet from a folder. A backlog in maths, circled in red. 'I cried for two days over this,' she said. 'I'm not perfect. I'm just a year ahead.' Ganga stared at the red circle. Nandini also told her to stop fetching dinner.

qa.q: What was circled in red on Nandini's marksheet?
qa.a: A backlog in maths was circled in red.

qa.q: What might Nandini be worried about when Ganga says 'You never get anything wrong'?
qa.a: Nandini is uneasy that Ganga sees her as flawless and leans on her too much, which could inflate her and burden Ganga.
Showing her own failed maths result and ending the dinner fetching, because honesty about flaws brought Ganga's picture of her down to earth.

qa.q: What is it like for Ganga to see the red circle?
qa.a: Ganga is likely surprised and relieved to learn someone she admires also failed, so her own failed test feels less shameful.

grounding: Shows a senior treated as flawless by a junior, who stays honest about her failures and refuses to use the admiration.

passage:
'Hansa-di, give me your lab record. I'll write it up tonight.'
'Why would you do that, Kalyani?'
'Because you're the captain. You're too important to waste time copying readings. Everyone says so.'
'Everyone is very kind. But I dropped two catches on Sunday, remember?'
'That was the sun! You're the best player this college has had.'
'Kalyani, sit for a second.' Hansa patted the pavilion step. 'I like that you look up to me. But if I let you do my record, I'd be using that. And I'd start believing I'm special.'
'You are, though.'
'I'm a decent bowler who's bad at chemistry and forgets to call her mother. Write your own record. If you want, we'll do them together after nets.'
Kalyani grinned, a bit embarrassed. 'After nets.'

qa.q: How many catches did Hansa drop on Sunday?
qa.a: Hansa dropped two catches on Sunday.

qa.q: What might Hansa worry about when Kalyani offers to write the record?
qa.a: Hansa is wary and a little uncomfortable, worried that saying yes would mean using Kalyani's admiration and starting to believe she is special.

qa.q: What would you advise a captain in Hansa's place?
qa.a: Be warm but honest about flaws, turn down favours that ride on admiration, and offer something fair instead, like doing records together after nets.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Hansa at the start?
qa.a: Kalyani sees Hansa as the best player the college has had, too important for ordinary chores, and even excuses the dropped catches.

grounding: Shows a captain whose junior treats her as perfect, and who admits her flaws and declines to use that admiration.
